keyTakeaways: South Korea's experience shows that audiences need to see exact surtitling languages, dates and ticket conditions before they book.

A 2020 study of 222 Chinese and Japanese respondents in South Korea linked lower Korean proficiency with greater willingness to attend subtitled performances; it did not measure European ticket sales.
Personal browser-based surtitles and a small reusable pool of loan phones can reduce initial equipment needs, but translation and staffing still cost money.

faq.question: Do East Asian tourists want to attend European theatre?
faq.answer: European tourism and heritage-interest data demonstrate a potential audience, not a measured European theatre conversion rate. The 2020 Korean study provides evidence that language access can affect stated interest in performances.

faq.question: Does a theatre need a subtitle screen at every seat?
faq.answer: No. Pockitle Cue Viewer works in a phone browser via link or QR code; a venue may supplement spectators' own devices with 10–20 affordable loan phones and spares, after testing the auditorium and network.

faq.question: Do translated surtitles replace accessibility captions?
faq.answer: No. Deaf and hard-of-hearing audience members may need identification of speakers and significant sounds. Venues must plan translation and accessibility services according to their audience's needs.

glossary.definition: Prepared translation shown in time with a staged performance.
On-screen text that may identify dialogue, speakers and meaningful sounds for deaf and hard-of-hearing audiences.
A venue-managed smartphone configured for spectators who need personal surtitles.
